stage: HISTORIE (engine stage 6) - fractal axis + competing frames - cache
disputedNote: Even where this story begins is disputed - picking a start date is itself a position. Frames change emphasis and annotation, never the record.

frames.label: June 2026 stabbing
frames.note: Under this frame the story opens with the knife attack in Belfast and the violent protests that followed within days. The record reads as a community reaction to a specific crime, with anti-racism rallies as the counter-response. This is the frame the victim's family and the wire-service news cycle open with.

frames.label: 2024 UK riots wave
frames.note: Under this frame the story opens with the Southampton and Britain-wide anti-immigration riots of the prior cycle. The record reads as a continuation of a post-incident mobilisation pattern across UK cities, not a one-off Belfast event. This is the frame anti-fascist outlets like Searchlight and Guardian UK-wide coverage open with.

frames.label: 1998 Good Friday Agreement
frames.note: Under this frame the story opens with the post-conflict settlement that froze but did not dissolve loyalist and nationalist community structures. The record reads as those structures finding new flashpoints in immigration disputes. This is the frame Northern Ireland political analysts and local commentators open with.

frames.label: 1968 Troubles onset
frames.note: Under this frame the story opens with the start of three decades of sectarian conflict in Northern Ireland. The record reads as the latest expression of lingering scars from a long unrest, with immigration the new fault line on old terrain. This is the frame Arab News-style historical commentary and academic observers open with.

bands.label: Stabbing and Belfast unrest
bands.summary: A stabbing in Belfast is followed by anti-immigration riots that injure police and by large anti-racism rallies across Northern Ireland and Britain.

nodes.title: Stabbing in Belfast precedes a week of disorder
nodes.what: A knife attack in Belfast preceded several days of anti-immigration street protests across the city. Coverage of the following week describes police injuries during violent disorder and a victim's family appealing publicly for calm.

nodes.title: Nigerian nurse reported attacked during Belfast unrest
nodes.what: A Nigerian nurse was reported attacked on her way home from work as anti-immigration violence continued in Belfast. The incident was cited in coverage of the wider pattern of attacks on migrants and visible minorities during the disorder.

nodes.title: Stabbing victim's family calls for calm
nodes.what: The family of the stabbing victim issued a public appeal for calm amid the violent anti-immigration protests in Northern Ireland. The appeal was widely circulated alongside coverage of police injuries and arrests.

nodes.title: Thousands attend anti-racism rally in Belfast
nodes.what: Thousands gathered in central Belfast for an anti-racism rally condemning the preceding days of anti-immigrant rioting. Organisers and speakers framed the event as a response to attacks on migrants and on police during the unrest.

nodes.title: Rival protesters clash in Glasgow and other UK cities
nodes.what: Anti-racism rallies were held in Glasgow, Brighton, Liverpool and Sheffield, where far-right and anti-racist protesters clashed. The UK-wide demonstrations were widely reported as a response to the Belfast riots.

nodes.title: Online amplification of the unrest draws scrutiny
nodes.what: Coverage of the Belfast disorder included accusations against high-profile online figures of fuelling the riots through social media posts. Reports detailed claims aimed at Elon Musk and Tommy Robinson by German state media and others.
nodes.disputed: Breitbart describes the accusations as German state media attacks on Musk and Robinson over their posts; Searchlight Magazine and Guardian-aligned coverage describe the same online activity as incitement that helped galvanise the anti-immigration mobilisation.

nodes.title: Anti-racism rallies continue into the weekend
nodes.what: Further anti-racism demonstrations were held across Northern Ireland and Britain a day after the main Belfast rally. Coverage emphasised the size of turnout and the continuing presence of counter-protests in several UK cities.

bands.label: UK anti-immigration riot wave
bands.summary: Southampton and other UK cities see post-incident anti-migrant protests and counter-mobilisations that set a template later read onto Belfast.

nodes.title: Stabbing at Southport dance class kills three children
nodes.what: A 17-year-old attacker killed three young girls and injured several other children and adults at a Taylor Swift themed dance workshop in Southport, Merseyside. The incident triggered immediate national grief and intense online speculation about the attacker's identity and motive, much of it inaccurate.

nodes.title: First anti-immigration riot outside Southport mosque
nodes.what: On the evening after the killings a crowd attacked a Southport mosque and clashed with police, injuring dozens of officers and damaging vehicles. False claims circulating on social media that the attacker was a Muslim asylum seeker were cited by police as a trigger for the violence.

nodes.title: Disorder spreads to English and Northern Irish towns
nodes.what: Over several days unrest spread to Sunderland, Hull, Liverpool, Rotherham, Middlesbrough, Belfast and other cities. Hotels housing asylum seekers were attacked, shops were looted and several hundred police officers were injured before arrests numbered in the high hundreds.
nodes.disputed: Some organisers and right-leaning commentators described the gatherings as legitimate protests against immigration policy; police, anti-racism groups and the government described them as racist riots fuelled by far-right networks online.

nodes.title: Anti-racism counter-mobilisations across the UK
nodes.what: Tens of thousands gathered in cities across Britain in counter-protests organised by Stand Up to Racism, trade unions and local groups, surrounding immigration advice centres and asylum hotels. Police reported that anticipated far-right gatherings that evening largely failed to materialise at the scale forecast on social media.

nodes.title: Fast-track courts hand down riot sentences
nodes.what: Courts began processing hundreds of arrests with rapid sentencing under the Crown Prosecution Service's disorder response. By the end of the month many defendants had received immediate custodial sentences for violent disorder, arson and racially aggravated offences linked to the unrest.

nodes.title: Southport attacker sentenced to minimum 52 years
nodes.what: Axel Rudakubana, who had pleaded guilty, was sentenced at Liverpool Crown Court for the murders and attempted murders. The court detailed his preparation and possession of extremist material, contradicting many of the identity-based claims that had circulated during the summer riots.

bands.label: Brexit era immigration politics
bands.summary: The Brexit vote and its aftermath reshape UK immigration debate and the Northern Ireland border arrangement, sharpening community-level disputes.

nodes.title: UK votes to leave the European Union
nodes.what: In a national referendum, 51.9 percent of UK voters chose to leave the EU. Northern Ireland voted 55.8 percent to remain, opening a gap between the regional vote and the UK-wide result. Immigration and border control were central themes of the Leave campaign.

cites.l: Wikipedia: 2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum

nodes.title: UK triggers Article 50
nodes.what: Prime Minister Theresa May formally notified the European Council of the UK's intention to withdraw, starting a two year negotiation. The Northern Ireland land border with the Republic became one of the most contested files. Free movement of EU citizens was identified as ending at withdrawal.

nodes.title: Northern Ireland Protocol agreed
nodes.what: London and Brussels concluded a revised withdrawal arrangement that kept Northern Ireland aligned with parts of the EU single market and customs rules to avoid a hard land border. Checks would instead apply on goods moving from Great Britain to Northern Ireland. Unionist parties opposed the deal as a sea border.
nodes.disputed: The UK government described the Protocol as a pragmatic solution protecting the Good Friday Agreement; the DUP and loyalist groups described it as a constitutional breach placing a customs frontier within the United Kingdom.

nodes.title: UK formally leaves the EU
nodes.what: The withdrawal agreement took effect and a transition period began during which EU rules continued to apply. Freedom of movement for new arrivals from the EU ended at the close of transition on 31 December 2020. A new points based immigration system was introduced.

nodes.title: Loyalist street violence in Belfast over the Protocol
nodes.what: Sustained rioting broke out in loyalist areas of Belfast and other Northern Ireland towns, with petrol bombs thrown at police and a bus hijacked and burned on the Shankill Road. Protesters cited the Irish Sea border created by the Protocol and policing decisions on a republican funeral. Dozens of police officers were injured over successive nights.

nodes.title: Windsor Framework replaces parts of the Protocol
nodes.what: Prime Minister Rishi Sunak and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a revised arrangement creating green and red lanes for goods entering Northern Ireland and a Stormont brake on new EU rules. The framework aimed to reduce checks while keeping the open land border. The DUP withheld support before later returning to power sharing in early 2024.

bands.label: Post-Good Friday settlement
bands.summary: The Good Friday Agreement formally ends the Troubles, but loyalist and nationalist community structures and intermittent street violence persist.

nodes.title: Good Friday Agreement signed in Belfast
nodes.what: British and Irish governments together with most Northern Ireland parties signed a multi-party accord establishing a power-sharing assembly, cross-border bodies and prisoner releases. The deal was endorsed by referendums in Northern Ireland and the Republic the following month. It formally ended the Troubles as an open conflict while leaving paramilitary structures and segregated communities largely in place.
nodes.disputed: Sinn Fein and the SDLP describe it as a settlement that secured equality and a path to a united Ireland by consent; the DUP and other unionist critics describe it as a deal that rewarded paramilitaries and weakened the union.

nodes.title: Omagh car bomb kills 29
nodes.what: A car bomb planted by the Real IRA, a dissident republican splinter group, detonated in the centre of Omagh, killing 29 people including a woman pregnant with twins. It was the single deadliest attack of the Troubles era and came months after the Good Friday Agreement. The bombing forced dissident republican factions onto the political and security agenda even as mainstream paramilitaries moved toward decommissioning.

cites.l: BBC On This Day: Omagh bomb

nodes.title: Holy Cross school dispute in north Belfast
nodes.what: Loyalist protests blocked Catholic primary school girls and their parents from walking to Holy Cross school through a Protestant area of Ardoyne, with confrontations continuing through the autumn. Police in riot gear escorted children past crowds throwing bottles, stones and a pipe bomb. The dispute became an emblem of how interface-area community tensions persisted after the Good Friday Agreement.

nodes.title: Provisional IRA orders end to armed campaign
nodes.what: The Provisional IRA leadership issued a public order to its units to dump arms and pursue exclusively political and democratic means. An independent commission confirmed decommissioning of weapons stocks later that year. The move removed a long-standing obstacle to restoring devolved government at Stormont.

nodes.title: Belfast City Hall flag vote sparks loyalist protests
nodes.what: Belfast City Council voted to limit flying of the Union flag over City Hall to designated days rather than year-round. Loyalist protests began outside the building that night and spread into months of street demonstrations, road blockades and rioting across Northern Ireland. Dozens of police officers were injured and hundreds of people were arrested over the following weeks.
nodes.disputed: Loyalist organisers describe the protests as defence of British identity and consent under the Agreement; nationalist and police commentary describes them as orchestrated disorder that drew in paramilitary-linked figures.

bands.label: The Troubles
bands.summary: Three decades of sectarian conflict in Northern Ireland shape policing, community geography and the patterns of street unrest still referenced today.

nodes.title: Derry civil rights march is baton-charged by police
nodes.what: A Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association march in Derry was blocked and dispersed by the Royal Ulster Constabulary, with officers using batons against marchers. The day is widely cited as a trigger point that escalated street confrontation into sustained unrest across Northern Ireland.

nodes.title: British troops deployed to Northern Ireland
nodes.what: After days of intercommunal violence in Belfast and Derry known as the Battle of the Bogside, the UK government ordered the deployment of British Army troops to Northern Ireland under Operation Banner. The deployment was initially framed as a short peacekeeping measure and became the longest continuous operation in British military history.

nodes.title: Bloody Sunday in Derry
nodes.what: British paratroopers shot dead 13 civil rights marchers in the Bogside area of Derry, with a fourteenth dying later from wounds. Initial military and government accounts were challenged for decades by survivors and victims' families.
nodes.disputed: The original Widgery Tribunal described the soldiers' actions as broadly justified by perceived threat; the later Saville Inquiry described the shootings as unjustified and the victims as posing no threat.

nodes.title: IRA announces ceasefire
nodes.what: The Provisional IRA announced a complete cessation of military operations, followed weeks later by a parallel ceasefire from the Combined Loyalist Military Command. The ceasefires opened the multi-party talks process that eventually produced the 1998 settlement, though the IRA ceasefire briefly broke down in 1996.

cites.l: BBC On This Day - IRA ceasefire

nodes.title: Good Friday Agreement reached in Belfast
nodes.what: Multi-party negotiations chaired by US senator George Mitchell produced the Belfast or Good Friday Agreement, setting up a power-sharing assembly, north-south institutions and provisions on policing, prisoners and decommissioning. Referendums in Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland endorsed the deal the following month.
